I want to discuss and possibly work on: finish, independently review, and safely hand off the uncommitted fix that makes Trail Context body updates fail closed when optimistic-concurrency verification fails.

Repository and working state

- Repository: entireio/cli.
- Reuse the existing branch and worktree named `fix-trail-context-overwrite`; do not create another branch or worktree.
- The branch was created from and tracks canonical `upstream/main`. At the start of the prior session, HEAD, `upstream/main`, and their merge base were all `8a43e78f1e7f8567e2bd77b058c5155893e58cb0`. Recheck this rather than assuming it is still current.
- Start the continuation session inside that CLI worktree. Do not associate the earlier Hub-repository session or its checkpoints with this CLI branch.
- Entire agent setup left two unrelated tracked diffs: a Claude metadata-read deny rule and a formatting-only rewrite of Entire settings. Inspect them carefully, but do not modify, stage, revert, or include them in the bug fix unless independently justified.
- Separate uncommitted Hub work exists on `feat/skill-workflow-hardening`, including an `update-trail-context` skill draft and eval artifacts. Do not touch it.
- The intended Trail fix is currently uncommitted. It changes the Trail API types, Trail update command logic, and focused Trail command tests. Use `git status` and `git diff` to identify the exact current state.

Begin with independent review

Before changing anything further, perform an extensive independent review and lead with findings plus a recommendation. Re-read all local repository/agent instructions and Entire Graph guidance. Use `entire graph search` as the first code-location move, then verify the relevant symbols and tests directly. Recheck canonical upstream, branch/worktree identity, local diffs, recent commits, and current GitHub issue/PR state. Decide independently whether the patch is correct, stale, already solved elsewhere, or broader than needed.

The safety invariant is: inability to establish the current Trail body version is not authority to replace it. A default body update must fail closed. Only an explicit `--overwrite` authorizes an unconditional replacement.

Relevant symbols are `resolveTrailUpdateBodyAtPath`, `runTrailUpdateWithClientAtPath`, and `sendTrailBody`. Review the Trail body request types and the focused Trail command tests around these symbols.

Historical and public context

- The unsafe behavior originated in merged PR #2079: https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2079
- Commit `d3f920f01270dfd9d7de3a0cdbcc08f4d4fcc320` introduced ETag/`If-Match` handling while preserving missing-ETag overwrite fallback.
- Commit `0dc4af34ddb446a855ba8a719867ad8960be5dd1` added a warning for a failed refetch while retaining the fallback.
- Checkpoint transcripts for those commits could not be retrieved locally. Describe the rationale as commit- and PR-backed intent, not transcript-backed intent.
- Live read-only searches in the prior session found no separate issue or newer exact fix. Recheck because that result can go stale. An older draft PR #1493, https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1493, covers a much broader update-by-number/ID/body-file design and contains an earlier interactive-read failure idea, but it was not a current canonical fix.
- No approved public issue for this exact bug was found. CONTRIBUTING requires an approved issue before a PR, so treat that as a blocker to public PR creation, not to local review or a local commit.

Reproduction and regression evidence already captured

The original unsafe test passed unchanged on canonical main with:

`GOCACHE=/private/tmp/entire-go-cache go test ./cmd/entire/cli -run '^TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureWarnsAndFallsBackToOverwrite$' -count=1 -v`

Exact output:

```
=== RUN   TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureWarnsAndFallsBackToOverwrite
=== PAUSE TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureWarnsAndFallsBackToOverwrite
=== CONT  TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureWarnsAndFallsBackToOverwrite
--- PASS: TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureWarnsAndFallsBackToOverwrite (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli  0.689s
```

That test proved a detail GET returning 500 still led to command success, `overwrite: true`, an empty `If-Match`, and a warning.

The test was then replaced with the focused regression `TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureSendsNoBodyWrite`. Before production changes it failed because the request counters observed one body PUT; the key failure was `Should be zero, but was 1`, followed by `FAIL` for that test and package. The test combines a metadata title update and a body update so it also proves a failed verification read causes neither a body PUT nor a preceding metadata PATCH. It expects an error containing `could not verify trail body is unchanged`.

An interactive regression, `TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_InteractiveBodyReadFailureSendsNoWrite`, also failed before production changes: the command proceeded toward the form after a detail 500 and returned nil instead of an error. It is intentionally not parallel because it controls process-wide stdin/environment.

Current proposed minimal patch

- In the interactive path, a detail/body seed read failure returns `could not load current trail body: %w` before opening the form or writing anything.
- In the non-interactive path, when a body update is requested without explicit overwrite, the detail/ETag verification happens before any metadata PATCH. A read failure returns `could not verify trail body is unchanged: %w`; it no longer warns and falls back to overwrite.
- `sendTrailBody` now sends `overwrite: true` only for explicit overwrite. With a nonempty ETag it sends `If-Match`. With no ETag and no explicit overwrite it sends neither, relying on the server's guarded semantics: an absent/empty body document can be created or cleared, while an existing nonempty body should conflict rather than be overwritten.
- The internal helper's now-unused error-writer parameter was removed and its test call sites updated.
- Tests were updated so missing ETag without explicit overwrite expects a guarded body request, explicit overwrite remains the negative control that skips the verification GET and sends overwrite authority, and the 409 conflict mapping remains covered.

Do not accept this design merely because it is already implemented. Independently verify the old-server/no-body-document contract. In particular, determine whether a successful detail response without an ETag is a legitimate absent-body case, whether sending neither `If-Match` nor overwrite is supported by old and current servers, and whether any server version interprets that request unsafely. If that assumption is not supported, stop and report the compatibility risk rather than widening the patch speculatively.

Also review:

- explicit `--overwrite` semantics and its guarantee that no verification GET is required;
- both non-interactive and interactive paths;
- partial metadata/body updates and the ordering that prevents metadata mutation before a failed body verification read;
- clearing an absent body document;
- 409 conflict behavior;
- whether any request can still mutate after a verification or seed read fails;
- whether the error messages follow repository conventions;
- whether removal of the internal error-writer parameter has unintended callers.

Passing evidence after the patch

The two regressions passed together:

```
=== RUN   TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureSendsNoBodyWrite
=== PAUSE TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureSendsNoBodyWrite
=== RUN   TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_InteractiveBodyReadFailureSendsNoWrite
--- PASS: TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_InteractiveBodyReadFailureSendsNoWrite (0.00s)
=== CONT  TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureSendsNoBodyWrite
--- PASS: TestRunTrailUpdateWithClient_EtagFetchFailureSendsNoBodyWrite (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli  0.840s
```

The final focused non-interactive run also passed in 0.900s. The narrow Trail update suite passed with:

`GOCACHE=/private/tmp/entire-go-cache go test ./cmd/entire/cli -run '^(TestResolveTrailUpdateBody_|TestRunTrailUpdate|TestSendTrailBody_)' -count=1`

The full CLI package passed with:

`GOCACHE=/private/tmp/entire-go-cache go test ./cmd/entire/cli -count=1`

`mise run fmt` followed by `mise run lint` passed; lint reported `0 issues`. `mise run dup` exited successfully but reported many pre-existing advisory 50-token duplicates, including existing Trail-test duplication, with no identified new blocker.

Preflight complication to resolve carefully

The repository-required `mise run check` was attempted in the real worktree. Its format/lint phase initially found one new `indent-error-flow` issue, which was fixed; the subsequent Trail tests passed. The full check then failed only because the unrelated Claude metadata-read deny diff makes `TestCommittedDogfoodSettingsIsCurrent` compare the locally changed checked-in configuration with installer output. Do not change that unrelated diff just to make the check green.

A disposable clean clone was used to apply only the Trail patch. Its format/lint phases passed, but full `test:ci` failed in two unrelated tests because the disposable clone's origin URL was a local bare-clone path rather than a GitHub remote. The failures were `TestSearchCmd_CodeFlagRequiresQuery` and `TestRunTrailListAll_PrintsLoginHintWhenNotLoggedIn`; both rejected or failed to parse that local origin. All Trail tests passed. The disposable clone and its temporary mise trust were cleaned up. The user prohibited changing remotes or settings, so do not normalize a remote to force a green check. Find a safe validation approach within those constraints, or report the environmental blocker precisely.

Work requested from the continuation

1. Report independent correctness findings and a recommendation before editing further.
2. If the current patch is sound, complete focused verification and repository-required checks as far as the unchanged unrelated diffs and remote constraints allow.
3. Run a correctness review, blast-radius review, and final code review. Verify that the tests observe the real write contract, not merely mocked return values.
4. Keep the patch narrow. Exact Trail-number/ID targeting, `--body-file`, post-write readback verification, the Hub `update-trail-context` skill, session-handoff changes, and broader workflow integration are follow-up slices unless this bug cannot be fixed safely without one.
5. Preserve the exact reproduction, red, green, and preflight evidence for a future reviewer-facing PR description and later workflow/blog notes.
6. Draft the PR body for review before any public mutation. Include the problem/causal story, compatibility tradeoff, safety invariant, exact validation, scoped non-goals, and the approved-issue prerequisite.
7. Follow the repository commit skill boundary: propose the scoped conventional commit and obtain any required confirmation before staging or committing. Stage only the intended Trail changes.

Constraints

- Do not authenticate Entire.
- Do not change remotes or settings.
- Do not require a live Trail for this unit-level fix.
- Do not run paid real-agent E2E tests. The Vogon canary is allowed only when repository checks require it.
- Do not modify, stage, revert, or bundle either unrelated configuration diff or any Hub work.
- Do not push, create or update a PR or Trail, create an issue, merge, close issues, label, or post public comments without explicit authorization.
- Call out stale assumptions, hidden compatibility risks, or evidence that should stop the work rather than papering over them.

Output order

- Independent review findings and recommendation.
- Reproduction and assessment of the minimal patch.
- Exact failing-then-passing regression evidence and broader validation.
- Correctness, blast-radius, and final review results.
- Remaining blockers, proposed commit, and a draft PR body, with no public mutation.

description: >
  Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical
  intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire
  skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
---

# Using Entire

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the
recorded intent, don't guess.**

Entire checkpoints capture the prompts, transcripts, and decisions behind every
agent-driven change. When you need to understand why code exists or how a module
evolved, look up the checkpoint history first. Only fall back to inference from
code structure when no history is available — and label that explicitly.

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

Also check whether the Entire Graph plugin is installed:

```bash
entire graph version
```

If it prints a version, the graph is available and **every code-locating step
in this skill must go through it** — never grep, find, or read whole files to
locate code when the graph can answer. The division of labor:

- **Structure** (where is X, what calls X, what breaks if X changes) → `entire graph`
- **Intent** (why is X like this, what was the developer thinking) → checkpoints

Graph command palette:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --format agent --top-k 5 \
  --query "<task in one sentence>"                                            # locate
entire graph def <symbol>                                                     # one definition
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in --format agent  # callers
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text                         # blast radius
entire graph commit <ref>                                                     # entity-level change list
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json                                    # semantic changes between refs
```

One search, then act — answer from the search output when it already suffices,
and read only a focused line range around reported locations. Skip the graph
when the task already names one small exact file. The full measured doctrine
lives in the `lean-mode` skill.

Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle: read focused source around the
reported `file:line` before relying on it. If `entire graph version` fails, the
plugin is absent — fall back to standard search tools without it.

## Scenario Routing

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|
| Locate or trace code structure | "where is X implemented" / "what calls X" / "what would changing X affect" / "find the code that does Y" | run `entire graph` directly (`search`, `def`, `neighbors`, `impact`) |
| Code block provenance | "why is this like this" / "wtf is going on" / "what happened at src/auth.ts:42" / "tell me why this changed" | `what-happened` |
| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |
| Recall a task playbook | "have we done this before" / "recall how we did X" / "how did we do this last time" | `recall` |
| Replay feature history | "replay <feature>" / "walk me through how X was built" / "show me the journey of Y" | `replay` |
| Teach a repo topic | "teach me <topic>" / "how does <topic> work in this repo" / "give me a lesson on X" | `entire-teach` |
| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |
| Generate a dispatch / summary | "summarize recent work" / "generate a dispatch" / "what was accomplished this week" | run `entire dispatch` directly |
| Code review with intent context | "review these changes" / "review this branch" / "audit before merging" | `entire-review` |
| Hand off to another agent | "hand off this session" / "continue in another agent" / "pick up the codex session" | `session-handoff` |
| Convert session to skill | "turn this into a skill" / "make a skill from this session" | `session-to-skill` |
| Link session to other repos | "link session to other repos" / "attach session to the foo repo" | `session-crosslink` |
| General exploration | "understand this module" / "explore how auth works" / "help me understand the codebase" | _(self — see below)_ |

If the scenario clearly maps to a sub-skill, delegate entirely to that skill's
workflow. Do not duplicate their steps here.

## General Exploration Flow

When no specific sub-skill fits — e.g. the user asks to "understand this
module" or "explore how auth works" — use this flow:

1. **Identify key files** in the target area with the graph when it is
   installed:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the module or behavior to understand>"
```

Then map the neighborhood of the top hits (`neighbors` for callers,
`impact` for blast radius) instead of reading whole files. Without the graph
plugin, identify entry points, main types, and core functions manually.

2. **Check for checkpoint coverage** on each key file:

```bash
git log --format='%H %s' -5 -- <file>
```

Look for `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailers in the commit bodies:

```bash
git log --format='%H %b' -5 -- <file> | grep -B1 'Entire-Checkpoint:'
```

3. **Read intent for covered commits** — extract the checkpoint ID from the
   trailer, then use JSON output for non-interactive consumption:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

If you only have a commit hash (not a checkpoint ID), use:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --no-pager
```

4. **Synthesize**: combine the recorded intent (from checkpoints) with the
   current code structure to build a comprehensive understanding.

5. **Report** your findings, clearly distinguishing:
   - Facts backed by checkpoint transcripts (label as "recorded intent")
   - Observations inferred from code alone (label as "inferred from code")

## AI Agent Usage Notes

When running Entire commands from an agent subprocess:

- **Always pass `--json`** for commands that support it and might prompt
  interactively. `--json` implies non-interactive output.
- **Always pass `--no-pager`** to prevent pager activation in subprocess
  contexts.
- **Always specify `--checkpoint <id>` or `--commit <sha>`** for
  `entire checkpoint explain` — without a locator, the command falls back to an
  interactive picker.

## When No Checkpoints Exist

If the target code predates Entire or has no checkpoint coverage:

1. Say explicitly: "No Entire checkpoint history is available for this code."
2. Proceed with standard code understanding — still graph-first when the
   plugin is installed (`entire graph search` to locate, `neighbors`/`impact`
   to trace call sites), reading focused source around the results; check git
   log for history.
3. Label all explanations as "inferred from code — not backed by recorded
   intent."
4. If the user wants deeper history, suggest `search` with related keywords —
   there may be checkpoints on related work even if the specific file isn't
   directly covered.

## Transparency Principle

Always make it clear whether your answer comes from:

- **Checkpoint-backed history** — you read the actual session transcript and
  know the developer's stated intent
- **Code inference** — you analyzed the code structure and are reasoning about
  probable intent

Never present inferred intent as if it were recorded fact. The core value of
this workflow is that distinction.

## References

For a deeper understanding of Entire's capabilities beyond what the sub-skills
cover, consult these resources:

- **CLI help**: run `entire help` to see all available commands and flags
- **Documentation**: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt — AI-friendly
  documentation index following the [llms.txt standard](https://llmstxt.org),
  designed to be consumed directly by LLMs and coding agents

# Correctness Review

**A change is correct when you can name who owns the write, what happens if the process stops on
either side of it, and which test fails on the old code through the real seam.** A diff that reads
well and passes CI has cleared neither bar.

Distilled from the August 2026 Entire CLI review corpus -- nine authored PRs, 40 initial human
inline findings across 244 reviewed PRs. Almost none of the expensive findings were syntax. They
were ownership, state classification, duplicated policy, and tests that watched a nearby
abstraction instead of the failure.

## Use When

- Before requesting review on your own change, or reviewing someone else's diff for correctness
  rather than style.
- The change touches lifecycle, sessions, checkpoints, persistence, hooks, auth, path resolution,
  locking, subprocesses, or files another tool owns.
- Not for abstraction quality and file growth -- that is `thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review`.
  Not for cost -- that is `perf-review`. Not for what breaks outside the diff -- that is
  `blast-radius`. This lens is about whether the change is *true*.

## The three questions

1. **Who owns the write?**
2. **What happens if the process stops immediately before or after the write?**
3. **Which test observes the real contract breaking on the old code?**

If any answer is vague, the change is not ready for review. Answer these first. Everything below
is how to get crisp answers.

## Do

1. **Map the state machine before judging a transition.** For lifecycle, checkpoint, hook, auth,
   or layout work, write the one-page model first: read owner, write owner, migration owner,
   recovery owner; durable state versus temporary state; the operation that makes it irreversible;
   the retry owner after each interruption point; the caller's time budget and every blocking call
   inside it; the user-visible state for success, partial success, and failure. Patching one
   transition without the table is the single most expensive mistake in the corpus.

2. **Trace failures to the outermost outcome.** Follow each new error, timeout, cancellation, and
   skipped operation through every caller to the command, hook, request, or job that the user
   observes. When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds),
   enumerate that caller chain with `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`
   (direct + transitive callers in one call) and verify against source — the graph can miss
   dynamic dispatch, so it bounds the trace rather than settling it. A safe helper can still be wrong when its error aborts an unrelated workflow. Do not
   approve an internal error policy until you can name the terminal exit status and user-visible
   result it produces.

3. **Audit interruption while resources are held.** For every state that owns a lock, transaction,
   pipe, temporary file, goroutine, or child process, cancel there and identify the cleanup path.
   Process exit is not proof that the domain operation succeeded. After failure, perform the next
   real operation that would expose leaked state; an error assertion alone does not prove cleanup.

4. **Separate safety, liveness, and fairness.** Prove independently that the change cannot corrupt
   state, can eventually make progress, and does not let one caller repeatedly jump queued callers.
   When a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess, or environment helper changes, compare callers
   with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline, and neither. A local fix that changes shared
   blocking or scheduling semantics has a wider contract than its motivating caller.

5. **Separate discovery from mutation authority.** Answer these apart, out loud: which file does
   the external tool read; which file may this command *inspect*; which file may this command
   *mutate*; who owns migration between them; what the user sees when those answers differ.
   Finding a path never grants permission to write to it.

6. **Classify states positively.** `absent` means the OS returned not-exist -- nothing else does.
   `unreadable`, `invalid`, `outdated`, `unresolved`, and `unsupported` are separate states with
   separate remedies. Unknown is not absent. Skipped is not success.

7. **Find the one owner of each decision.** If two functions answer the same eligibility question,
   make them call one predicate. Short duplicated policy is more dangerous than long duplicated
   formatting: one condition drifts and ownership or recovery silently changes. Search by
   responsibility and invariant, not by the symbol name you were about to add.

8. **Push the fix to the deepest boundary that can enforce the invariant once for all callers.**
   Normalize where data becomes permanent rather than pretending the current writer is the only
   producer. Preserve the wire format while you do it.

9. **Prove the test is real.** It fails on the old code for the reported reason, enters through the
   production seam that owns the behavior, and asserts the durable artifact or external result --
   not an intermediate value. Add a negative control. Cover every backend that owns the same
   contract. Use the real `git`, the real protocol, the real lock when that is the source of truth.

10. **Trace every claim to the branch that makes it true.** Comments, status text, warnings,
   remedies, and the PR body are part of the contract. If a message says "removed", a mutation
   happened. If a remedy says "run X", X can fix this exact state. Name the actual recovery owner.

11. **Walk the edge-case matrix** in `references/edge-case-matrix.md` for the categories the change
   touches. These are ordinary Git, filesystem, process, and terminal states, not exotic ones.

12. **Treat every automated finding as a hypothesis.** Reproduce it, check the module's language and
   tool versions, and reply with the mechanism. Do not change correct code to satisfy a linter bot
   working from an outdated model of the language.

13. **Re-scope the moment review changes the ownership model.** Stop patching the old shape. Split
    discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration into separate changes whose
    ownership decisions can be reviewed independently.

`references/failure-patterns.md` has the seven recurring shapes with worked examples. Scan for them
by name; each one is a finding when present:

- a transition patched without its state machine;
- write ownership inferred from path proximity;
- an error collapsed into absence, or a skip reported as success;
- the same decision ladder in two places;
- a test on a nearby abstraction instead of the production failure;

# Using Entire

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the
recorded intent, don't guess.**

Entire checkpoints capture the prompts, transcripts, and decisions behind every
agent-driven change. When you need to understand why code exists or how a module
evolved, look up the checkpoint history first. Only fall back to inference from
code structure when no history is available — and label that explicitly.

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

Also check whether the Entire Graph plugin is installed:

```bash
entire graph version
```

If it prints a version, the graph is available and **every code-locating step
in this skill must go through it** — never grep, find, or read whole files to
locate code when the graph can answer. The division of labor:

- **Structure** (where is X, what calls X, what breaks if X changes) → `entire graph`
- **Intent** (why is X like this, what was the developer thinking) → checkpoints

Graph command palette:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --format agent --top-k 5 \
  --query "<task in one sentence>"                                            # locate
entire graph def <symbol>                                                     # one definition
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in --format agent  # callers
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text                         # blast radius
entire graph commit <ref>                                                     # entity-level change list
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json                                    # semantic changes between refs
```

and read only a focused line range around reported locations. Skip the graph
when the task already names one small exact file. The full measured doctrine
lives in the `lean-mode` skill.

Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle: read focused source around the
reported `file:line` before relying on it. If `entire graph version` fails, the
plugin is absent — fall back to standard search tools without it.

## Scenario Routing

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|
| Locate or trace code structure | "where is X implemented" / "what calls X" / "what would changing X affect" / "find the code that does Y" | run `entire graph` directly (`search`, `def`, `neighbors`, `impact`) |

| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |

| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |
| Generate a dispatch / summary | "summarize recent work" / "generate a dispatch" / "what was accomplished this week" | run `entire dispatch` directly |

module" or "explore how auth works" — use this flow:

   installed:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the module or behavior to understand>"
```

`impact` for blast radius) instead of reading whole files. Without the graph
plugin, identify entry points, main types, and core functions manually.

2. **Check for checkpoint coverage** on each key file:

```bash
git log --format='%H %s' -5 -- <file>
```

```bash
git log --format='%H %b' -5 -- <file> | grep -B1 'Entire-Checkpoint:'
```

   trailer, then use JSON output for non-interactive consumption:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --no-pager
```

   current code structure to build a comprehensive understanding.

   - Facts backed by checkpoint transcripts (label as "recorded intent")
   - Observations inferred from code alone (label as "inferred from code")

When running Entire commands from an agent subprocess:

- **Always pass `--json`** for commands that support it and might prompt
  interactively. `--json` implies non-interactive output.
- **Always pass `--no-pager`** to prevent pager activation in subprocess
  contexts.
- **Always specify `--checkpoint <id>` or `--commit <sha>`** for
  `entire checkpoint explain` — without a locator, the command falls back to an
  interactive picker.

## When No Checkpoints Exist

If the target code predates Entire or has no checkpoint coverage:

1. Say explicitly: "No Entire checkpoint history is available for this code."
2. Proceed with standard code understanding — still graph-first when the
   plugin is installed (`entire graph search` to locate, `neighbors`/`impact`
   to trace call sites), reading focused source around the results; check git
   log for history.
3. Label all explanations as "inferred from code — not backed by recorded
   intent."
4. If the user wants deeper history, suggest `search` with related keywords —
   there may be checkpoints on related work even if the specific file isn't
   directly covered.

## Transparency Principle

Always make it clear whether your answer comes from:

- **Checkpoint-backed history** — you read the actual session transcript and
  know the developer's stated intent
- **Code inference** — you analyzed the code structure and are reasoning about
  probable intent

Never present inferred intent as if it were recorded fact. The core value of
this workflow is that distinction.

## References

For a deeper understanding of Entire's capabilities beyond what the sub-skills
cover, consult these resources:

- **CLI help**: run `entire help` to see all available commands and flags
- **Documentation**: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt — AI-friendly
  documentation index following the [llms.txt standard](https://llmstxt.org),
  designed to be consumed directly by LLMs and coding agents

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

Also check whether the Entire Graph plugin is installed:

```bash
entire graph version
```

If it prints a version, the graph is available and **every code-locating step
in this skill must go through it** — never grep, find, or read whole files to
locate code when the graph can answer. The division of labor:

- **Structure** (where is X, what calls X, what breaks if X changes) → `entire graph`
- **Intent** (why is X like this, what was the developer thinking) → checkpoints

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --format agent --top-k 5 \
  --query "<task in one sentence>"                                            # locate
entire graph def <symbol>                                                     # one definition
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in --format agent  # callers
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text                         # blast radius
entire graph commit <ref>                                                     # entity-level change list
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json                                    # semantic changes between refs
```

One search, then act — answer from the search output when it already suffices,
and read only a focused line range around reported locations. Skip the graph
when the task already names one small exact file. The full measured doctrine
lives in the `lean-mode` skill.

Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle: read focused source around the
reported `file:line` before relying on it. If `entire graph version` fails, the
plugin is absent — fall back to standard search tools without it.

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|

| Code block provenance | "why is this like this" / "wtf is going on" / "what happened at src/auth.ts:42" / "tell me why this changed" | `what-happened` |
| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |
| Recall a task playbook | "have we done this before" / "recall how we did X" / "how did we do this last time" | `recall` |
| Replay feature history | "replay <feature>" / "walk me through how X was built" / "show me the journey of Y" | `replay` |
| Teach a repo topic | "teach me <topic>" / "how does <topic> work in this repo" / "give me a lesson on X" | `entire-teach` |
| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |

# Edge-case matrix

Walk the categories the change touches. These are ordinary states, not exotic ones -- every row
below appeared as a real review finding or a real bug.

## Git and paths

- [ ] Normal checkout
- [ ] Conventional linked worktree
- [ ] `.bare/worktrees` layout
- [ ] Separate Git directory
- [ ] Ordinary submodule
- [ ] Linked submodule
- [ ] Symlinked checkout or directory
- [ ] Symlinked final file, and dangling symlink
- [ ] Missing, unreadable, malformed, and non-regular paths
- [ ] Path containment still holds *after* symlink resolution
- [ ] No remote, fork remote, raw URL, multiple push URLs, elected remote

## State and persistence

- [ ] Absent
- [ ] User-owned but not managed by this tool
- [ ] Partial
- [ ] Current
- [ ] Outdated
- [ ] Invalid
- [ ] Unreadable
- [ ] Unresolved
- [ ] Unsupported
- [ ] Older persisted format
- [ ] Unknown fields preserved on rewrite
- [ ] Nil versus empty serialized values (`null` versus `[]`)

## Process and concurrency

- [ ] Cancellation before the durable write
- [ ] Cancellation during each state that holds an external resource or prepared transaction
- [ ] Cancellation after the write but before state save
- [ ] Graceful abort releases locks, temporary files, pipes, goroutines, and child processes
- [ ] The next real operation succeeds immediately after cancellation or failure
- [ ] Lock contention and lock timeout
- [ ] Safety, liveness, and fairness evaluated separately
- [ ] Deadline-bearing, cancelable-without-deadline, and non-cancelable callers retain their contract
- [ ] Shared blocking, polling, or retry changes audited across all caller classes
- [ ] Concurrent writer from another process (the real one, not an in-process stand-in)
- [ ] Cleanup that removes state a later step needs
- [ ] Retry after a partial operation
- [ ] Idempotent rerun

## Environment and user interaction

- [ ] Variable unset
- [ ] Variable present but empty
- [ ] Tool-specific inherited variables cannot override the explicitly selected target
- [ ] Ambient variables poisoned in tests to prove repository, config, and credential isolation
- [ ] No TTY
- [ ] Raw-mode TTY
- [ ] `NO_COLOR` or non-styled output
- [ ] Windows and missing POSIX shell
- [ ] Expired, missing, and explicitly selected login contexts

## Failure semantics

- [ ] Typed sentinel errors matched with `errors.Is`, never by string
- [ ] Presence distinguished from a non-empty value (`os.LookupEnv`)
- [ ] Caller cancellation propagated separately from a child timeout
- [ ] Process exit success distinguished from domain-operation success
- [ ] Protocol response, process result, and local cancellation state agree
- [ ] Internal timeout or contention traced to the outermost command, hook, request, or job result
- [ ] Contention or temporary unavailability is not reported as a data conflict
- [ ] Context-aware lock acquisition wherever a context exists
- [ ] The underlying error preserved unless the public contract deliberately replaces it
- [ ] A silent-error type used only when the command already printed the user-facing error
- [ ] Unreadable, malformed, or unresolved never turned into absent
- [ ] No success reported after skipping every requested target

## User-visible contract

- [ ] Every status has a distinct meaning
- [ ] Every success message follows a confirmed success
- [ ] Every warning names the affected path, remote, context, or agent when that helps
- [ ] Every remedy can fix the exact state that printed it
- [ ] The command does not print the same error twice
- [ ] Comments and docs name the actual recovery owner and execution path

## Test hygiene

- [ ] Focused test shown failing on the old code, then passing
- [ ] Entry through the production seam, not a nearby helper
- [ ] Outermost affected workflow result asserted, not only the helper's return value
- [ ] Assertion on the durable artifact or external result
- [ ] Aftermath checked with the next real operation that would expose leaked state
- [ ] Negative control proving unrelated behavior did not change
- [ ] Every backend that owns the same contract covered
- [ ] Native tooling or the real protocol used where it is the source of truth
- [ ] Real lock held, or the real competing operation run, for concurrency claims
- [ ] Related log fields asserted on the same record
- [ ] Raw serialized bytes asserted when encoding shape is part of the contract
- [ ] Parallel by default, except where the test mutates process-global state
- [ ] Isolated temporary repository, config directory, cache, and token storage
- [ ] No spawned binary inherits an interactive terminal

## Language-level choices that encode semantics (Go)

- Keep `ctx` bound to the caller context; name a derived timeout for its purpose
  (`discoveryCtx`), never shadow the caller's.
- Distinguish `os.ErrNotExist` from permission and I/O errors.
- Keep atomic writes, containment validation, and symlink policy together -- atomic replacement
  alone does not define safe ownership.
- Preserve file modes and unknown fields when editing user-owned configuration.
- Create a happens-before edge with a channel, mutex, or atomic in race-tested code.
- Treat `exec.Cmd.Wait` as a process result, not proof that a child protocol committed its operation.
- Inspect `exec.Cmd.Cancel` before using the default kill behavior for a stateful child protocol.
- Record local cancellation state when a cooperative child abort can still exit successfully.
- Close resources at the right lifetime boundary; a cleanup that deletes state is not the same
  operation as terminating a process.
- Check the module's language version before accepting syntax advice.
# Correctness failure patterns

The seven shapes the strongest review comments kept finding. Each entry: what it looks like, a
worked example from the corpus, and what to do instead.

## 1. A transition patched without its state machine

The idea is right, the adjacent transitions are wrong.

Reserving a checkpoint ID before an interruptible write so recovery reuses the same identity was
correct. What review found around it: reservation and condensation each decided independently
whether a session had content; the new state mutation added a blocking lock inside a three-second
`SessionEnd` budget; a task-only session could have `StepCount == 0` and no shadow branch yet still
hold durable work; a comment named the post-commit path as the retry owner when `doctor` owned
that recovery case.

**Instead:** write the transition table first -- phase, files, transcript content, task records,
durable writes, identity, retry owner, cancellation timing. Two functions answering the same
eligibility question must call one predicate.

## 2. Write ownership inferred from path proximity

An external tool reads its config from the root checkout; the command may be invoked from a linked
worktree. Treating the discovered path as a natural mutation target was unsafe in six distinct
ways: a derived root could resolve to `$HOME`, a tool's home directory, a bare repository's parent,
or somewhere outside the checkout; a directory or file symlink could redirect the write; a scratch
worktree could modify a tracked file belonging to another checkout; an unreadable file could be
reported as successfully removed; repository-wide hooks could stay active while the picker called
the agent absent; a valid root-checkout setup drew the same warning as a broken one.

**Instead:** answer read / inspect / mutate / migrate / explain as five separate questions.
Discovery does not grant mutation authority.

## 3. An error collapsed into absence, or a skip reported as success

Every `stat` error treated as "file absent". Invalid JSON treated as outdated config that `--force`
can repair. Any ref-read error treated as a missing ref. A configuration error swallowed so a
feature silently disabled itself. A command reporting success after skipping the only selected
target.

**Instead:** the six positive states, each with its own output and remedy.

| State | Means | Wrong to say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| absent | the OS returned not-exist | anything else |
| unreadable | the path may exist; the read failed | absent |
| invalid | bytes read, schema not satisfied | outdated, or absent |
| outdated | valid state on an older contract | invalid |
| unresolved | cannot prove which resource applies | absent, or a guess |
| unsupported | layout understood, deliberately not handled | broken |

## 4. The same decision ladder in two places

Two eager-condensation eligibility ladders in one PR. A new Git worktree traversal added beside
three existing implementations. Repeated settings loads, duplicated remote rules, and tests that
re-stated production assumptions instead of calling them.

**Instead:** one policy decision, one function. Duplication is most dangerous when the code is
short and encodes policy -- two six-line predicates beat two fifty-line formatters as a hazard,
because a one-condition drift silently moves ownership or recovery.

## 5. A test on a nearby abstraction instead of the production failure

Every one of these shipped as a "passing" test that could not have caught the bug:

- asserting a helper's model instead of the remote's `HEAD`, which is the source of truth;
- covering one checkpoint backend when the bug lived at the shared permanent write boundary;
- unmarshaling JSON when the bug *is* the raw `null` versus `[]` encoding;
- simulating a competing writer in-process when production competition is native `git update-ref`
  in another process;
- exercising a lock helper without proving the read-modify-write section holds the lock;
- stubbing cancellation as `context.Canceled` when production wraps an `*exec.ExitError` as
  `signal: killed`;
- claiming a logged-out regression while both runs used `loggedIn=true`;
- checking that a warning and a component field appeared *somewhere* in a log rather than on the
  same record.

**Instead:** fails on the old code for the reported reason; enters through the production seam;
asserts the external contract or durable artifact. Plus a negative control, and every backend that
owns the contract.

## 6. Output, a comment, or a PR claim the code does not guarantee

A docs pipeline that claimed image externalization on a path that never ran it. A comment naming
the wrong retry owner. A status describing configured behavior as active behavior. A hint
recommending a flag the command did not have.

**Instead:** treat user output and invariant comments as code. Re-read them after the code changes.
Keep proven facts and hypotheses separate in the PR body, and state any wire-format, API,
performance, security, or migration effect.

## 7. One diff carrying an unsettled contract

The costliest PR in the corpus accumulated 42 commits answering discovery, ownership, mutation,
migration, trust, diagnostics, setup, and CI at once. Size was not the problem -- the repository
merges large changes routinely. Scope *before the contract is stable* was.

The safer sequence: pin the external tool's real behavior with an integration test; add read-only
discovery and diagnostics; agree on mutation ownership; add mutation only if still needed; handle
migration and consolidation separately.

**Instead:** the diff solves one causal problem, can be reverted without reverting unrelated
behavior, and hides no product or ownership question inside its implementation.

## Automated review is a hypothesis generator

Of 333 bot inline findings, 89 drew replies and many produced real fixes around cancellation, path
traversal, races, user output, and test isolation. It also produced confident false positives:
`range` over an integer called a compile error (valid since Go 1.22, and the module is on 1.26); a
`t.Parallel` loop-variable capture that current range semantics already fixed; an assumption about
the `exhaustive` linter's `default` handling that the repository's own config contradicted.

Reproduce the claim and check the configured tool version before changing correct code.

## The habits that worked

Worth repeating deliberately: splitting a PR when root cause and boundary hardening were different
claims; preserving `null` versus `[]` and testing raw JSON because ordinary unmarshaling erased the
distinction; answering review by writing out the full lifecycle model and asking for correction;
anchoring a design to the external tool's real behavior with a pinned integration test; red-green
TDD with a non-exempt control record and cross-provider blast-radius checks; keeping a UI fix
narrow and reusing the shared helper; rejecting a wrong review suggestion with evidence.

The goal is not zero review findings. It is moving the expensive ones -- ownership, recovery,
mutation authority -- into design work before the diff exists.

d8c8936a3bfbf34629e057ad29eeae32f26fb43c
trail create: stop inheriting stdin for the branch push

Addresses a finding on the trail. The justification the comment gave —
git prompting for credentials as it would on a push the user typed —
does not hold. git push has no --stdin mode; git's own credential prompt
uses /dev/tty or askpass; the OPF prompt reads /dev/tty via bubbletea's
fallback; and the hook never receives our stdin anyway, since git hands
it a pipe carrying the ref list.

So the only effect was to replace an immediate EOF with a real blocking
read. A non-interactive trail create — an agent whose stdin is a
long-lived pipe rather than a closed fd — could park on a prompt until
trailBranchPushTimeout instead of failing fast. Left at /dev/null, which
is where it was before the streaming change.

Deliberately does not touch cancellation: the orphaned-hook cost is
recorded as accepted in trailBranchPushTimeout's note, and killing the
process group would reverse that decision, not refine it.

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M1Y7QH20GVSQGG0CRGYC1DJ0

e7efe875c67f4945126ef120aacd9105cdf3f2cf
Say what the push timeout actually kills, and what a pipe would cost

The known-limitation note on trailBranchPushTimeout claimed expiry kills git
mid-rewrite. It kills git, but not the rewrite: CommandContext's default Cancel
is Process.Kill() on the child PID, no Setpgid is set, and the OPF re-redaction
and ref CAS-updates run in the pre-push hook — a grandchild. The hook is
orphaned, not interrupted, so the StatusWalkBudget failure mode (SIGKILL on the
process holding the lock) does not transfer here. Record the orphan as the cost
that is actually being accepted, and why killing the group would be worse.

Second note: the *os.File requirement is load-bearing for more than the tty.
With a pipe interposed, Cmd.Wait blocks on its copy goroutine until every
holder of the write end closes, an orphaned hook holds one, and WaitDelay is
unset — so a pager on the root command would leave this call unbounded, which
is the one thing the timeout exists to prevent.

Comments only; no behaviour change.

d8c8936a3bfbf34629e057ad29eeae32f26fb43c
trail create: stop inheriting stdin for the branch push

Addresses a finding on the trail. The justification the comment gave —
git prompting for credentials as it would on a push the user typed —
does not hold. git push has no --stdin mode; git's own credential prompt
uses /dev/tty or askpass; the OPF prompt reads /dev/tty via bubbletea's
fallback; and the hook never receives our stdin anyway, since git hands
it a pipe carrying the ref list.

So the only effect was to replace an immediate EOF with a real blocking
read. A non-interactive trail create — an agent whose stdin is a
long-lived pipe rather than a closed fd — could park on a prompt until
trailBranchPushTimeout instead of failing fast. Left at /dev/null, which
is where it was before the streaming change.

Deliberately does not touch cancellation: the orphaned-hook cost is
recorded as accepted in trailBranchPushTimeout's note, and killing the
process group would reverse that decision, not refine it.

e7efe875c67f4945126ef120aacd9105cdf3f2cf
Say what the push timeout actually kills, and what a pipe would cost

The known-limitation note on trailBranchPushTimeout claimed expiry kills git
mid-rewrite. It kills git, but not the rewrite: CommandContext's default Cancel
is Process.Kill() on the child PID, no Setpgid is set, and the OPF re-redaction
and ref CAS-updates run in the pre-push hook — a grandchild. The hook is
orphaned, not interrupted, so the StatusWalkBudget failure mode (SIGKILL on the
process holding the lock) does not transfer here. Record the orphan as the cost
that is actually being accepted, and why killing the group would be worse.

Second note: the *os.File requirement is load-bearing for more than the tty.
With a pipe interposed, Cmd.Wait blocks on its copy goroutine until every
holder of the write end closes, an orphaned hook holds one, and WaitDelay is
unset — so a pager on the root command would leave this call unbounded, which
is the one thing the timeout exists to prevent.

Comments only; no behaviour change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

9d4a5d18958568344775998215d5441f4167de1d rename(cli): entire trail command tree -> entire change
ENT-1890: rename the CLI's `entire trail` command family to `entire
change`, matching the client-side half of the trail->change rename
(no alias — `trail` is reserved for the slice-2 container commands).

Renames trail_*_cmd.go -> change_*_cmd.go (and the api package's wire
types trail_types.go/trail_review_types.go/trail_thread_types.go ->
change_*.go), the command constructors and their user-facing Use/Short/
Long/error text, and the API path/JSON-field spellings that move with
it: /api/v1/trails/... -> /api/v1/changes/..., trailId/trailNumber ->
changeId/changeNumber, and the browser link the CLI prints ->
/{owner}/{repo}/changes/{n}.

The shared cmd/entire/cli/trail domain package (trail.Metadata,
trail.Status, ...) is intentionally NOT renamed — it is internal
representation, not part of the command's user-facing name, and stays
out of this file-rename's scope; the two files that reference it
(change_cmd.go, api/change_types.go) import it under a `change` alias
so the renamed code reads consistently.

This is atomic by necessity (same rationale as the entire-api
trail->change PRs): a partial rename leaves half the command tree
calling functions the other half just renamed, so it lands as one
large, mechanical diff rather than several small ones.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/REDACTED

---
d3f920f01270dfd9d7de3a0cdbcc08f4d4fcc320 feat(trail): use If-Match etag for trail body writes instead of always overwriting
`trail update --body` now reads the description's etag and sends it as
If-Match, so a body write is rejected (412) rather than silently
clobbering a description that changed since it was read. A new
--overwrite flag opts into the old unconditional-replace behavior, and
a missing etag (older server, no body document, or a failed
best-effort read) gracefully falls back to Overwrite rather than
refusing.
